meta.location: Zarahemla, the east seashore cities, and the land Bountiful
principles: A vote that settles a dispute and does not end it
Refusal to fight as a political act
A campaign ended by one man in a tent

world_behind.title: The quarrel starts over particular points of law
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says a part of the people wanted a few points altered, and verse 3 says Pahoran refused. Mormon never says which points.

world_behind.title: Both sides get names
world_behind.text: Verse 5 names the king-men, verse 6 the freemen. Mormon defines each by what it wanted rather than by who led it.

world_behind.title: The vote settles it
world_behind.text: Verse 7 has the voice of the people decide for the freemen. Mosiah 29 had set up exactly this mechanism, and it works.

world_behind.title: The losers refuse to serve
world_behind.text: Verse 13 has the king-men welcome the invasion and keep their weapons down, out of anger at the chief judge and at those who had voted with him.

world_behind.title: Moroni asks for authority before using force
world_behind.text: Verse 15 has him send a petition with the voice of the people, and verse 16 says it was granted according to that voice. Mosiah 29:26 is the constitutional rule he is invoking, that the voice of the people decides. The killing in verse 18 follows a grant made under it.

world_behind.title: Amalickiah's oath is flagged as rash
world_behind.text: Verse 9 recalls the oath to drink Moroni's blood and verse 10 calls the promise rash before the chapter shows why. Alma 49:27 records the swearing itself two chapters earlier, and Alma 51:34 has Teancum put a javelin through him in his sleep.

world_behind.title: The Lamanites take six cities
world_behind.text: Verses 22 through 26 list Moroni, Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, and Mulek. Alma 50:13 to 15 records three of those cities being founded a decade earlier, and Alma 62:14 to 26 records the last of them being taken back. The internal dispute cost the coastline for eleven chapters.

words.text: Those who wanted a king. The compound occurs eleven times in this record and never in the King James Bible, and Alma 60 and 62 return to it. Mormon defines them by their aim: to alter the law and overthrow the free government.
Those who wanted the free government kept. Seven uses here, none in the King James Bible. Mormon says they had sworn to maintain their rights and their religion by a free government.

Hasty, spoken without weighing it. It appears once in the record, and twice in the King James Bible, where Ecclesiastes warns against being rash with the mouth before God. Mormon applies it to Amalickiah's oath and lets the chapter prove him right.

High birth, and the claim that goes with it. Its count is three here, none in the King James Bible, all inside this chapter. Verse 21 says those who professed the blood of nobility were brought down to humble themselves like their brethren.

A name or designation. The word occurs once in scripture. Mormon uses it to say that afterward nobody was known by the name king-men, which makes the suppression a matter of the label as well as the faction.
A light throwing spear. The word turns up three times here, and the King James Bible seven, five of them of Saul throwing one at David. Teancum uses it at close range on a sleeping man.

phrases.term: A few particular points of the law should be altered
phrases.text: Mormon describes the demand and withholds its content. The reader never learns which points, only that Pahoran would not move and that the refusal produced a party.

phrases.term: Those who were desirous that Pahoran should be dethroned from the judgment-seat were called king-men
phrases.text: The name is given with the aim attached. Mormon names the faction in the same sentence that says they wanted a king established over the land.

phrases.term: This matter of their contention was settled by the voice of the people
phrases.text: The mechanism from Mosiah 29 doing its work. The vote goes to the freemen, Pahoran keeps the seat, and the king-men are put to silence.

phrases.term: This was a critical time for such contentions to be among the people of Nephi
phrases.text: Mormon states the timing problem directly. Amalickiah is arming while Zarahemla argues, and the next fifteen verses are the cost of the overlap.

phrases.term: He had sworn to drink the blood of Moroni
phrases.text: An oath recorded so its failure can be recorded. Verse 10 calls it rash, and verse 34 has Amalickiah killed in his sleep by a man he never met in battle.

phrases.term: They were glad in their hearts; and they refused to take up arms
phrases.text: The king-men welcome an invasion. Mormon gives the reason as anger at the chief judge and the people of liberty, which makes the refusal a continuation of the vote by other means.

phrases.term: Give him power to compel those dissenters to defend their country or to put them to death
phrases.text: Moroni asks for the authority in writing, with the voice of the people behind it. The record is careful to show the request before the action.

phrases.term: To pull down their pride and their nobility and level them with the earth
phrases.text: The order as given, with an alternative attached: or they should take up arms and support the cause of liberty. Verse 20 says most of them took the second option.

phrases.term: There were four thousand of those dissenters who were hewn down by the sword
phrases.text: The count. Mormon adds that the surviving leaders were imprisoned because there was no time for trials, which marks the irregularity without excusing it.

phrases.term: Were compelled to hoist the title of liberty upon their towers
phrases.text: The banner of Alma 46 raised under compulsion. Mormon records that the sign of a voluntary covenant was flown by men who had a sword at their backs.

phrases.term: Teancum stole privily into the tent of the king, and put a javelin to his heart
phrases.text: The campaign ends in one sentence. Mormon gives no speech, no confrontation, and no comment, and closes the chapter with the days of Amalickiah ended.

verses.label: v. 2–6
verses.title: Two names built out of one relative clause
verses.text: The record makes the parties by repeating a phrase and then attaching a label to it. Those who were desirous that opens verses 4, 5 and 6, and appears in no other three verses of the volume. The law should be altered does the same work, standing in verses 2, 4 and 5 and nowhere else. Out of that repetition come the two names: the first group "were called king-men," the second "took upon them the name of freemen." One side is named by others and the other names itself, and the difference is in the verbs.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: A constitutional crisis handled in two clauses
verses.text: "This matter of their contention was settled by the voice of the people. And it came to pass that the voice of the people came in favor of the freemen." No count is given, no procedure described, no speech quoted, and no date supplied beyond the year already named in verse 1. Five verses go to a single assassination later on; the vote gets two clauses. What the record does supply is the outcome's fragility, since the losing side is still there in verse 13.

verses.label: v. 8
verses.title: One clause of social analysis
verses.text: Between the vote and the invasion the record stops to say who the king-men were: "those who were in favor of kings were those of high birth, and they sought to be kings; and they were supported by those who sought power and authority over the people." Two groups are distinguished inside one party, those who wanted thrones and those who wanted patrons. It is the only sentence in the chapter that explains a motive instead of reporting an act, and nothing later in the chapter depends on it.

verses.label: v. 13
verses.title: What they felt, not only what they did
verses.text: The king-men refuse to defend the country, and the record does not leave it at refusal: hearing that the Lamanites were coming, "they were glad in their hearts; and they refused to take up arms." Gladness is not needed to explain anything that follows. The military fact would be complete without it. Its presence turns a constitutional faction into people with an attitude toward invasion, and it is the last thing said about them before Moroni asks for power to compel them.

verses.label: v. 15–21
verses.title: The one number in the chapter
verses.text: Moroni does not begin with force. Verse 15 has him send a petition "with the voice of the people, unto the governor of the land," asking to be given authority. Only then does verse 17 order the attack, and verse 19 gives the result: "there were four thousand of those dissenters who were hewn down by the sword." That is the only figure the chapter reports, and it counts his own countrymen killed by his own army. Verse 21 states the objective in terms of vocabulary: "there were not any known by the appellation of king-men." The campaign ends when a word stops being used.

verses.label: v. 26–27
verses.title: Six cities in a row, and who built the walls
verses.text: City is used thirteen times here and all thirteen fall between verses 23 and 26. Verse 26 lists the captures without a pause between them: Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, Mulek. Verse 27 then adds the detail that makes the list bitter, that these were "all of which were strongly fortified after the manner of the fortifications of Moroni." The defences that made the cities worth taking are the ones the man losing them designed.

verses.label: v. 33–37
verses.title: A year and a man ended together
verses.text: The killing takes four verses and no dialogue: Teancum and one servant go out, sleep "had overpowered" the camp, a javelin, a return, and men woken up and told. Then the chapter closes on a doubled formula, "thus endeth the twenty and fifth year of the reign of the judges over the people of Nephi; and thus endeth the days of Amalickiah." The twenty and fifth year stands in three verses of the whole volume, and all three are in this chapter, at verses 1, 12 and 37. The year is named when it opens, again when the invasion begins, and a third time to close both it and the man.

chapter.title: A working vote does not end the quarrel
chapter.text: The voice of the people settles the matter in verse 7, and the losing side sabotages the war effort in verse 13. Mormon shows the mechanism functioning and being outlasted.

chapter.title: The content of the dispute is withheld
chapter.text: A few particular points of the law, never specified. Mormon keeps the reader's attention on what the factions did rather than on who had the better case.

chapter.title: Refusal to serve is treated as an act of war
chapter.text: The king-men do nothing and the coastline falls. The chapter's structure puts the suppression and the loss of six cities side by side.

chapter.title: Moroni gets authority before he uses force
chapter.text: The petition, the voice of the people, the grant, and then the march. Mormon records the sequence carefully in a chapter where four thousand die.

chapter.title: The record notes the irregularity
chapter.text: Leaders imprisoned without trial because there was no time. Mormon states it plainly and does not defend it.

chapter.title: A voluntary banner is raised by compulsion
chapter.text: The title of liberty goes up on the towers of men who were given a choice between it and the sword. Alma 46 had them running to it freely.

chapter.title: The rash oath frames the ending
chapter.text: Amalickiah swears to drink Moroni's blood in verse 9 and dies in verse 34 without ever reaching him. Mormon flags the oath as rash twenty-five verses early.

chapter.title: The chapter ends without commentary
chapter.text: A javelin, a return, a guard set, and the year closed. Mormon gives the death of the book's most capable villain in four verses and adds nothing.

applications.title: Hold the rule when the pressure is procedural
applications.text: Pahoran would not alter the law and would not hearken to the petitions asking him to alter it. Some requests should be received and refused, since a process that can be petitioned into rewriting its own rules is not much of a process.

applications.title: Take your name from what you defend
applications.text: The freemen were called by what they had covenanted to maintain, not by the party they were arguing with. A group defined only by its opponent runs out of purpose on the day the opponent does.

applications.title: Notice when the timing is the real problem
applications.text: The dispute would have been survivable at another moment. Ask whether your current argument is worth having now, given what else is happening.

applications.title: Weigh an oath before you swear it
applications.text: Amalickiah promised something spectacular and died without doing it. Say what you will actually do, and leave the dramatic version unsaid.

applications.title: Accept the outcome of the vote you took part in
applications.text: The king-men lost and then withheld their help. When a decision goes against you in a process you agreed to, the question is what you do next.

applications.title: Get the authority before you use the power
applications.text: Moroni put his request on paper and had the people stand behind it. When you are about to do something drastic and defensible, make sure the authorization exists first.

applications.title: Write down what the emergency suspended
applications.text: The leaders who survived went to prison because there was no time for their trials at that period. Crises push ordinary procedure aside; keep a list of what got set down, so that someone remembers to pick it back up.

applications.title: Expect good work to be used against you
applications.text: The cities Amalickiah took were strongly fortified after the manner of Moroni, and those fortifications then sheltered the Lamanites. Anything built well enough is worth capturing, so plan for the day what you made is in somebody else's hands.

questions.text: What have I refused to alter, and is it principle or stubbornness?
When did a decision go against me, and how did I behave afterward?
Have I ever been quietly glad about trouble that would hurt people I resent?
What am I about to do that I should get permission for?
Where have I skipped a proper process because there was no time?
What have I displayed publicly that I do not hold privately?
What claim about myself would I have to give up to be humbled like my brethren?
